Poverty For Profit

By: Harri Vithi | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When poverty is repackaged for profit

Unique Selling Point:
This is a story about how billions of Rands are spent to "upgrade" poverty

Summary:
The Money
Across South Africa, over R7 billion has been allocated this year alone to upgrade informal settlements.
Jumpas Informal Settlement, in Denver, east of Johannesburg, is one of the beneficiaries. R75 million was allocated for electrification. On paper, it’s a development story - an informal settlement upgrade.
On the ground, only 64 concrete poles and a mini-substation stood — while thousands of residents remained without electricity. Until Cllr Neuren Petersen began highlighting the issue in 2025.
The question emerges:
Where is the money going?


The Letter
At the centre of the story is a letter written by the project’s Community Liaison Officer, Masande Madikane — written while he was still free.
In it, he names contractors and officials.
He describes an alleged secret meeting at Mike’s Kitchen in Parktown where beneficiaries were reportedly pre-selected.
He details intimidation and alleged bribery attempts.
The letter becomes our roadmap.
We follow the names.
We test the claims.
We trace the money.
But as the allegations surface, tension escalates inside the settlement.


The Violence
Jumpas has seen three murders in the past year — including the killing of Masande’s mother, a community activist who opposed shack farming.
Masande reported threats. Masked men in a blue car allegedly targeted him.
After his mother’s murder, allegations emerged that he had been seen disguised as a zama-zama — allegedly to avenge her. He was later arrested and charged with murder.
But the letter alleging corruption came first.
So the central question remains:
Is Jumpas a crime story?
Or is it a corruption story wrapped in crime?


Further information:
2. Interviews:

Cllr Neuren Pietersen - DA - Masande gave Pietersen the letter on the alleged rot at Jumpas…which he handed over to a Hawks investigator. Seemingly, no investigation took place but shortly thereafter, the murders began…

Gogo Muriel - informal settlement resident - brief interview (hidden identity) we’ll film off site in the area using an actor as most people are extremely jittery as they say they’re receiving threats from zama-zamas in the informal settlement. Allegedly, they’re worried that the legitimization of the informal settlement will disrupt their digging

Gugulethu Sangweni - insight into factional tenderpreneur battles in the local ANC branch


Accountability

Those who were present at the allegedly clandestine meeting:

Sipho Mthembu - Johannesburg Water Non-Executive Director and Former Chairperson - accused of running a construction mafia in the area. He’s the ANC Ward 118 chair and scores tenders in the area - a conflict of interest? Apparently, one needs to be close to him to score a tender.

Ben Matiko - City Power - almost zero internet presence. What was he doing at that meeting?

Maqhinga Mbatha - security company owner, allegedly went to Masanda’s office in a huff and instructed him to tear up Mxolisi Phindani’s company profile. The same Mxolisi Phindani discussed at the table who was not to benefit from the Jumpas project and landed up with nine bullets - dead. In addition, Masanda accused Maqhinga’s brother - Ayanda Mbatha - of threatening to kill him.

Ngcebo Ngubane - Ward Committee Member; why is he allegedly attending meetings where tenders are being pre-determined

Moeketsi Mpetha - the main contractor on Jumpas - Ompetha Power Projects

3. We’ll film at Jumpas Informal Settlement in Cleveland - day and night.

4. Drone - we can secure permission from several business owners who weren’t informed about the project in the first place

5. Reenactments - please advise on budget for actors. Scenarios: restaurant meeting, letter writing in shack and zama-zama disguise

Script:


(Neuren Pietersen) So you see this is a house.
(Claire Mawisa) The size compared to where they're going.
(Neuren Pietersen) It’s tiny but this is three, four, five - so this is twenty five square meters.
(Claire Mawisa) Named after the goldmine that operated here over a century ago, Jumpers informal settlement is home to over a thousand people.
(Claire Mawisa) Two years ago, a multi-million-rand project was approved, to provide electricity, sanitation and housing.
(Claire Mawisa) Are you trying to tell me a family is supposed to be living in here?

(Neuren Pietersen) Yes, for a family from one to ten people.
(Claire Mawisa) But when we visit with ward councillor Neuren Pietersen, there’s little sign of the alleged improvements.
(Claire Mawisa) I can see right into this unit. I'm thinking of the wind of the rain, the heat in summer, the cold in winte
(Claire Mawisa) The site is prone to flooding, and is still zoned for mining: in fact, below ground… zama zamas tunnel for gold.
(Neuren Pitersen) So that makes it very difficult to formalize a situation because we've heard lots of horrific stories, especially from the East Strand of gun fights, etcetra with them protecting their turf.
(Claire Mawisa) But illegal mining and poor service don’t explain the atmosphere of fear that hangs over this place.
(Anonymous Source) There are so many things that are still happening but we're just going to be keeping quiet because we also don't want to be killed.
(Claire Mawisa) As we investigate we uncover a darker story of alleged corruption, intimidation, and even murder.
(Claire Mawisa) Across South Africa’s informal settlements, billions of Rand are allocated to upgrade settlements just like these.
(Claire Mawisa) Joburg’s utility company, City Power, says it’s so far spent more than R50 million on site. But how and where has that money been spent?
(Claire Mawisa) Building specialist, Heather Trumble, spent 23 years with the City of Joburg.
(Heather Trumble) City power may have spent 50 million, but certainly not on that site.
(Heather Trumble) What we are seeing here is that the inflation of the electrification of the shacks are in fact tripled.
(Claire Mawisa) City Power says it costs R35 000 - R 49 000 to electrify each shack, substantially more than what Trumble believes the cost should be.
(Heather Trumble) Going back to what an average house looks at, it shouldn't be more than in between R 15 000 - 20 000.
(Claire Mawisa) And yet City Power claims to be spending around R15 thousand per shack more than that… on what is still planned as a temporary site.
(Claire Mawisa) Quibbling over a few thousand Rand per shack might seem insignificant, but there are millions available for the Jumpers upgrade; rich pickings for anyone wanting to make a quick buck.
(Claire Mawisa) And a mysterious letter detailing a string of sinister events, including several killings, suggests that’s exactly what’s at stake.
(Claire Mawisa) It alleges clandestine meetings, intimidation — and even murder. All linked to a supposed scramble for money connected to this project.
(Claire Mawisa) When the Jumpers upgrade began two years ago, a so-called community liaison officer, or CLO, was appointed to represent locals.
(Claire Mawisa) Just six months later, in a letter to Pietersen, the CLO made shocking claims against the project contractors. It was this correspondence that opened Pandora’s Box.
(Claire Mawisa) The letter was a bit of a shocking read.
(Neuren Pietersen) It goes into a lot of detail of being asked to attend a private meeting between himself and the local known tenderpreneurs in the area.
(Claire Mawisa) That meeting is alleged to have happened in Joburg’s northern suburbs, and according to the CLO, it was attended by several businessmen demanding contracts at Jumpers. His letter describes a negotiation about which companies would receive contracts for security and sanitation - and which would be excluded.
(Heather Trumble) It's clearly designed so that what happens is that a particular group or company will then get the contract. And so they can then inflate the price.
(Claire Mawisa) Our research, including off-camera interviews, reveals a pattern.
(Anonymous Source) Hey, these mafias! I can say these projects are dominated by the members of the ANC.
(Anonymous Source) They actually capture the one who leads the project. They capture them!
(Producer) Who are they?
(Anonymous Source) The Chairperson of the ANC. Sipho Mthembu.
(Claire Mawisa) Too scared to talk on camera, our sources none-the-less provide a name: Sipho Mthembu: former chair of Joburg Water, now a non-executive director. He’s also branch chair of the ANC in the ward in which Jumpers falls.
(Claire Mawisa)The CLO’s letter claims that anyone who wants to do business in the ward has to be close to Mthembu.
(Letter) Mthembu promised me that I'll get a bonus of R50 000 from the main contractor if I do as they say…
(Claire Mawisa) We call Mthembu, and he admits to regular meetings at a Joburg restaurant.
(Sipho Mthembu) I have a lot of meetings in different places including *bleep restaurant name*, but to accuse me - whoever is accusing me is not telling the truth.
(Claire Mawisa) What involvement then in construction do you have in Ward 118?
(Sipho Mthembu) Number one, I don’t have a construction company - that’s number one. My interest is to make sure that our people that are unemployed - especially young people they get employment on whatever projects is coming to our area.
(Claire Mawisa) But Mthembu was the director of a construction company for at least a decade and, what’s more, records show he attended Jumpers project meetings on behalf of that company for more than a year after resigning as director.
(Claire Mawisa) The letter goes on to name others who attended the gathering with Mthembu:
(Letter) I also do not trust the main contractor because him and Ben from City Power were part of that secret meeting and the main contractor always stands up for these guys as if he is scared of them.
(Claire Mawisa) Moeketsi Mpeta
(Neuren Pietersen) He's the main contractor. He's doing, you know, installing the poles, putting the slabs, building the houses.
(Claire Mawisa) Ben Matiko
(Neuren Pietersen) He works for City Power. I think he’s a stakeholder manager.
(Claire Mawisa) City Power plays a central role in the Jumpers upgrade, so we arrange an interview with spokesperson Isaac Mangena.
(Isaac Mangena) I'm not aware of any promises or efforts to influence that were made.
(Claire Mawisa) But even if it doesn't have influence, just his presence at a meeting, if something off color is being discussed, his presence at that meeting almost endorses whatever is being spoken about.
(Isaac Mangena) No, no - that’s why I’m saying that would be worrying for us and that's why I say that I will definitely make sure that I look into it.
(Claire Mawisa) City Power later confirms at least one staff member was present at the stakeholder meeting, but denies any improper conduct.
(Claire Mawisa) But influencing contracts isn’t the most serious alleged crime surrounding the Jumpers project. With millions of Rands up for grabs through the manipulation of service delivery contracts, murder inevitably enters the discussion.
(Heather Trumble) The bigger the project is, the bigger the, the mafia, the construction mafia around and they will threaten everybody. And yes, there's been many stories of people having a hit on them.
(Letter) There have been some strange men that drove in a blue Corolla who went around looking for me.They all wore face masks and were too scary.
(Claire Mawisa) The CLO confided in Pietersen that he was intimidated when trying to report the alleged corruption to police.
(Neuren Pietersen) He expressed a lot of concern about reporting this issue at the Cleveland Police station. He believed that there were people that were watching him.
(Claire Mawisa) Then, in the months that followed, a number of people connected to the project were murdered.
(Claire Mawisa) A contractor the letter says was excluded from the project was shot dead. The CLO’s mother was killed. And now, shockingly, the CLO himself stands accused of murder.
(Neuren Pietersen) He's been arrested. He's now in jail and apparently for murdering one of the people that murdered his mother.
(Claire Mawisa) What would you say to people who say or believe you are an influential man and a dangerous man?
(Sipho Mthembu) I’m not surprised if I find such accusations. I think it’s politically motivated - I’m not dangerous any how. I’m just a leader of the ANC.
(Claire Mawisa) While our sources state Mthembu is the mastermind of this alleged construction mafia, they did not implicate him directly in any violent acts or murders.
(Claire Mawisa) When news of our investigation got out, Pietersen received a message saying: “You deserve to be killed.”
(Claire Mawisa) When systems meant to uplift seem to exploit instead, is this development at all, or simply poverty repackaged for profit?

(Claire Mawisa) When news of our investigation got out, Pietersen received a message saying: “You deserve to be killed.” (Claire Mawisa) When systems meant to uplift seem to exploit instead, is this development at all, or simply poverty repackaged for profit?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When poverty is repackaged for profit
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This is a story about how billions of Rands are spent to "upgrade" poverty
metadata.Summary: The Money Across South Africa, over R7 billion has been allocated this year alone to upgrade informal settlements. Jumpas Informal Settlement, in Denver, east of Johannesburg, is one of the beneficiaries. R75 million was allocated for electrification. On paper, it’s a development story - an informal settlement upgrade. On the ground, only 64 concrete poles and a mini-substation stood — while thousands of residents remained without electricity. Until Cllr Neuren Petersen began highlighting the issue in 2025. The question emerges: Where is the money going? The Letter At the centre of the story is a letter written by the project’s Community Liaison Officer, Masande Madikane — written while he was still free. In it, he names contractors and officials. He describes an alleged secret meeting at Mike’s Kitchen in Parktown where beneficiaries were reportedly pre-selected. He details intimidation and alleged bribery attempts. The letter becomes our roadmap. We follow the names. We test the claims. We trace the money. But as the allegations surface, tension escalates inside the settlement. The Violence Jumpas has seen three murders in the past year — including the killing of Masande’s mother, a community activist who opposed shack farming. Masande reported threats. Masked men in a blue car allegedly targeted him. After his mother’s murder, allegations emerged that he had been seen disguised as a zama-zama — allegedly to avenge her. He was later arrested and charged with murder. But the letter alleging corruption came first. So the central question remains: Is Jumpas a crime story? Or is it a corruption story wrapped in crime?
